**Penelope** ([/pəˈnɛləpi/](/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[[1]](#cite_note-1) [*pə-NEL-ə-pee*](/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"); [Ancient Greek](/wiki/Ancient_Greek "Ancient Greek"): Πηνελόπεια, *Pēnelópeia*, or Πηνελόπη, *Pēnelópē*)[[2]](#cite_note-2) is a character in [Homer](/wiki/Homer "Homer")'s *[Odyssey](/wiki/Odyssey "Odyssey").* She was the queen of [Ithaca](/wiki/Homer%27s_Ithaca "Homer's Ithaca") and was the daughter of Spartan king [Icarius](/wiki/Icarius_(Spartan) "Icarius (Spartan)") and Naiad [Periboea](/wiki/Periboea "Periboea")[[3]](#cite_note-3).The mythological Penelope is known for her fidelity to her husband [Odysseus](/wiki/Odysseus "Odysseus"), despite the attention of more than a hundred [suitors](/wiki/Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") during his absence. In one source, Penelope's original name was Arnacia or Arnaea.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

Etymology
---------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Penelope&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology")]

[Glossed](/wiki/Gloss_(annotation) "Gloss (annotation)") by [Hesychius](/wiki/Hesychius_of_Alexandria "Hesychius of Alexandria") as "some kind of bird"[[5]](#cite_note-5) (today arbitrarily identified with the [Eurasian wigeon](/wiki/Eurasian_wigeon "Eurasian wigeon"), to which [Linnaeus](/wiki/Carl_Linnaeus "Carl Linnaeus") gave the binomial *Anas penelope*), where *-elōps* (-έλωψ) is a common Pre-Greek suffix for predatory animals;[[6]](#cite_note-6) however, the semantic relation between the proper name and the gloss is not clear. In [folk etymology](/wiki/Folk_etymology "Folk etymology"), *Pēnelopē* (Πηνελόπη) is usually understood to combine the Greek word *pēnē* (πήνη), "[weft](/wiki/Weft "Weft")", and *ōps* (ὤψ), "face", which is considered the most appropriate for a cunning weaver whose motivation is hard to decipher.[[7]](#cite_note-7) [Robert S. P. Beekes](/wiki/Robert_S._P._Beekes "Robert S. P. Beekes") believed the name to be [Pre-Greek](/wiki/Pre-Greek "Pre-Greek") and related to *pēnelops* (πηνέλοψ)[[8]](#cite_note-8) or *pēnelōps* (πηνέλωψ).

Role in *The Odyssey*
---------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Penelope&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Role in The Odyssey")]

Penelope is married to the main character, the king of [Ithaca](/wiki/Homer%27s_Ithaca "Homer's Ithaca"), [Odysseus](/wiki/Odysseus "Odysseus") (Ulysses in Roman mythology), and daughter of [Icarius](/wiki/Icarius_(Spartan) "Icarius (Spartan)") of [Sparta](/wiki/Sparta "Sparta") and [Periboea](/wiki/Periboea "Periboea") (other alternatives being [Polycaste](/wiki/Polycaste "Polycaste")[[9]](#cite_note-9) or [Asterodia](/wiki/Asterodia "Asterodia")[[10]](#cite_note-10)). She has only one son with Odysseus, [Telemachus](/wiki/Telemachus "Telemachus"), who was born just before Odysseus was called to fight in the [Trojan War](/wiki/Trojan_War "Trojan War"). She waits twenty years for Odysseus's return, during which time she devises various cunning strategies to delay marrying any of the 108 [suitors](/wiki/Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope") (led by [Antinous](/wiki/Antinous_son_of_Eupeithes "Antinous son of Eupeithes") and including [Agelaus](/wiki/Agelaus "Agelaus"), [Amphinomus](/wiki/Amphinomus "Amphinomus"), Ctessippus, [Demoptolemus](/wiki/Demoptolemus "Demoptolemus"), [Elatus](/wiki/Elatus "Elatus"), Euryades, [Eurymachus](/wiki/Eurymachus "Eurymachus") and [Peisander](/wiki/Peisander_(mythology) "Peisander (mythology)")).[[11]](#cite_note-11)[[a]](#cite_note-12)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/55/Penelope_and_the_Suitors_-_John_William_Waterhouse_-_ABDAG003035.jpg/250px-Penelope_and_the_Suitors_-_John_William_Waterhouse_-_ABDAG003035.jpg)](/wiki/File:Penelope_and_the_Suitors_-_John_William_Waterhouse_-_ABDAG003035.jpg)

*Penelope and the Suitors* by [John William Waterhouse](/wiki/John_William_Waterhouse "John William Waterhouse") (1911-1912)

On Odysseus's return, disguised as an old beggar, he finds that Penelope has remained faithful. She has devised cunning tricks to delay the suitors, one of which is to pretend to be weaving a burial shroud for Odysseus's elderly father [Laertes](/wiki/Laertes_(father_of_Odysseus) "Laertes (father of Odysseus)") and claiming that she will choose a suitor when she has finished. Every night for three years, she undoes part of the shroud, until [Melantho](/wiki/Melantho "Melantho"), a slave, discovers her subterfuge and reveals it to the suitors.[[12]](#cite_note-13)

Penelope's efforts to delay remarriage is often seen as a symbol of marital fidelity to her husband, Odysseus.[[13]](#cite_note-Mackail-1916-14) But because [Athena](/wiki/Athena "Athena") wants her "to show herself to the wooers, that she might set their hearts a-flutter and win greater honor from her husband and her son than heretofore", Penelope does eventually appear before the suitors.[[13]](#cite_note-Mackail-1916-14)(xviii 160−162)

Irene de Jong wrote:

>  As so often, it is Athena who takes the initiative in giving the story a new direction ... Usually the motives of mortal and god coincide, here they do not: Athena wants Penelope to fan the Suitors' desire for her and (thereby) make her more esteemed by her husband and son; Penelope has no real motive ... she simply feels an unprecedented impulse to meet the men she so loathes ... adding that she might take this opportunity to talk to [Telemachus](/wiki/Telemachus "Telemachus") (which she will indeed do).[[14]](#cite_note-15)

It is important to consider the alternate perspective of Penelope entertaining, and even enjoying the attention of, her suitors. Italian philosophy historian [Giula Sissa](/w/index.php?title=Giula_Sissa&action=edit&redlink=1 "Giula Sissa (page does not exist)") offers a unique perspective which supports this idea. The Odyssey allows room for Penelope’s identity free of being Odysseus' wife. As she awaits his return, she makes a plan to deal with her suitors while also responding to her desires. Sissa discusses how Penelope gives her suitors the opportunity to demonstrate themselves as the best candidate for her attention. Sissa writes,

> Penelope innovates. And she does so because she responds in the same register to the desires of the men who have been awaiting her verdict for three years. This is an erotic desire to which she reacts, first, with seductive wiles of messages and promises, and then by inviting them to demonstrate their excellence, not in terms of wealth and social prestige, but in terms of something extremely personal and physical. In order to please Penelope, they have to be on par with Ulysses in showing the might of their bodies.[[15]](#cite_note-16)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b1/Achamanid-Woman-Statue-Persia-Persepolis.jpg/250px-Achamanid-Woman-Statue-Persia-Persepolis.jpg)](/wiki/File:Achamanid-Woman-Statue-Persia-Persepolis.jpg)

Among the four surviving statues of Penelope, [this](/wiki/Statue_of_Penelope "Statue of Penelope") is the oldest dating back to the 5th century BC, crafted 300 years after [Homer](/wiki/Homer "Homer") composed [The Odyssey](/wiki/Odyssey "Odyssey"). Discovered in [Persepolis](/wiki/Persepolis "Persepolis") and housed at [National Museum of Iran](/wiki/National_Museum_of_Iran "National Museum of Iran"), the other three are kept at [Vatican Museum](/wiki/Vatican_Museums "Vatican Museums") and [Capitoline Museum](/wiki/Capitoline_Museums "Capitoline Museums") in [Rome](/wiki/Rome "Rome").[[16]](#cite_note-17)[[17]](#cite_note-18)[[18]](#cite_note-19)

She is ambivalent, variously asking [Artemis](/wiki/Artemis "Artemis") to kill her and apparently considering marrying one of the suitors. When the disguised Odysseus returns, she announces in her long interview with him that whoever can string Odysseus's rigid bow and shoot an arrow through twelve axe heads may have her hand. "For the plot of the *Odyssey*, of course, her decision is the turning point, the move that makes possible the long-predicted triumph of the returning hero".[[19]](#cite_note-20)

There is debate as to whether Penelope knows that it is Odysseus. Penelope and the suitors know that Odysseus (were he in fact present) would easily surpass them all in any test of masculine skill, so she may have started the contest as an opportunity for him to reveal his identity. On the other hand, because Odysseus seems to be the only person (except, perhaps, Telemachus) who can actually use the bow, she could just be further delaying her marriage to one of the suitors.[[20]](#cite_note-21)

When the contest of the bow begins, none of the suitors are able to string the bow, except Odysseus who wins the contest. Having done so, he proceeds to slaughter the suitors – beginning with Antinous whom he finds drinking from his cup – with help from Telemachus, Athena and the slaves [Eumaeus](/wiki/Eumaeus "Eumaeus") the swineherd and [Philoetius](/wiki/Philoetius "Philoetius") the cowherd. Odysseus has now revealed himself in all his glory (with a little makeover by Athena); yet Penelope cannot believe that her husband has really returned – she fears that it is perhaps some god in disguise, as in the story of [Alcmene](/wiki/Alcmene "Alcmene") – and tests him by ordering her slave [Eurycleia](/wiki/Euryclea "Euryclea") to move the bed in their bridal-chamber. Odysseus protests that this cannot be done, since he made the bed himself and knows that one of its legs is a living [olive tree](/wiki/Olive_tree "Olive tree"). Penelope finally accepts that he truly is Odysseus, a moment that highlights their *homophrosýnē* (ὁμοφροσύνη, "like-mindedness").[[21]](#cite_note-22) Homer implies that from then on Odysseus would live a long and happy life together with Penelope and Telemachus, wisely ruling his kingdom, and enjoying wide respect and much success.[[22]](#cite_note-23)

Role in other myths
-------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Penelope&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Role in other myths")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/59/Ring_Penelope_CdM_Luynes_515.jpg/250px-Ring_Penelope_CdM_Luynes_515.jpg)](/wiki/File:Ring_Penelope_CdM_Luynes_515.jpg)

Gold [intaglio](/wiki/Intaglio_(jewellery) "Intaglio (jewellery)") ring, Syria, last quarter of the 5th century BC ([Louvre Museum](/wiki/Louvre_Museum "Louvre Museum"))

Penelope also appears in the lost Greek epic *[Telegony](/wiki/Telegony "Telegony")* that does not survive except in a summary, but that was attributed to [Eugamon](/wiki/Eugamon "Eugamon") or Eugammon of Cyrene and written as a sequel to the *[Odyssey](/wiki/Odyssey "Odyssey")*. According to this epic, Odysseus had a son called Telegonus with [Circe](/wiki/Circe "Circe") when he was on her island. When Telegonus had grown to manhood, Circe sent him in search of Odysseus. Shipwrecked on Ithaca by a storm, Telegonus misidentified the island and, assailed by hunger, began plundering it. Odysseus and his oldest son, [Telemachus](/wiki/Telemachus "Telemachus"), defended their city and, in the ensuing melée, Telegonus accidentally killed his father with a lance tipped with the venomous spine of a [stingray](/wiki/Common_stingray "Common stingray"). After discovering the identity of his father, Telegonus brought Telemachus and Penelope to Circe's island. Here, Athena ordered the marriage of Telemachus to Telegonus's mother, the enchantress Circe, while Telegonus married the new widowed Penelope. After burying Odysseus, Circe made the other three immortal.[[23]](#cite_note-24) According to [Hyginus](/wiki/Gaius_Julius_Hyginus "Gaius Julius Hyginus"), Penelope and Telegonus had a son called [Italus](/wiki/Italus "Italus") who, according to some accounts, gave his name to [Italy](/wiki/Italy "Italy").[[24]](#cite_note-:0-25) This legend inspired [Sophocles](/wiki/Sophocles "Sophocles")'s lost tragedy *[Odysseus Acanthoplex](/wiki/Odysseus_Acanthoplex "Odysseus Acanthoplex")*.

In some early sources such as [Pindar](/wiki/Pindar "Pindar"), [Pan](/wiki/Pan_(god) "Pan (god)")'s parents are [Apollo](/wiki/Apollo "Apollo") and Penelope.[[25]](#cite_note-26) [Herodotus](/wiki/Herodotus "Herodotus"),[[26]](#cite_note-27) [Cicero](/wiki/Cicero "Cicero"),[[27]](#cite_note-28) [Apollodorus](/wiki/Bibliotheca_(Pseudo-Apollodorus) "Bibliotheca (Pseudo-Apollodorus)"),[[28]](#cite_note-29) and [Hyginus](/wiki/Gaius_Julius_Hyginus "Gaius Julius Hyginus")[[29]](#cite_note-30) all describe Hermes and Penelope as his parents. [Pausanias](/wiki/Pausanias_(geographer) "Pausanias (geographer)")[[30]](#cite_note-31) records the story that Penelope had in fact been unfaithful to Odysseus, who banished her to Mantineia upon his return. In the 5th century AD [Nonnus](/wiki/Nonnus "Nonnus")[[31]](#cite_note-32) names Pan's mother as Penelope of [Mantineia](/wiki/Mantineia "Mantineia") in [Arcadia](/wiki/Arcadia_(region) "Arcadia (region)"). Other sources[[32]](#cite_note-33) report that Penelope had slept with all 108 suitors in Odysseus's absence, and gave birth to Pan as a result.[[33]](#cite_note-34) This myth reflects the [folk etymology](/wiki/Folk_etymology "Folk etymology") that equates Pan's name (Πάν) with the Greek word for "all" (πᾶν).[[b]](#cite_note-35) The *Odyssey* carefully suppresses this variant tradition.[[34]](#cite_note-36)

Iconography
-----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Penelope&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Iconography")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/00/EB1911_Tapestry_-_Fig._3.png/250px-EB1911_Tapestry_-_Fig._3.png)](/wiki/File:EB1911_Tapestry_-_Fig._3.png)

Drawing of a depiction on an Ancient Greek pottery vessel. Penelope sits before a tapestry on a [warp-weighted loom](/wiki/Warp-weighted_loom "Warp-weighted loom")

Penelope is recognizable in Greek and Roman works, from Attic vase-paintings—the [Penelope Painter](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/category:Penelope_Painter "commons:category:Penelope Painter") is recognized by his representations of her—to Roman sculptures copying or improvising upon classical Greek models, by her seated pose, by her reflective gesture of leaning her cheek on her hand, and by her protectively crossed legs, reflecting her long chastity in Odysseus's absence, an unusual pose in any other figure.[[35]](#cite_note-37)

Latin tradition
---------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Penelope&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Latin tradition")]

Latin references to Penelope revolved around her sexual loyalty to the absent Odysseus. It suited the marital aspect of Roman society representing the tranquility of the worthy family.[[36]](#cite_note-38) She is mentioned by various classical authors including [Plautus](/wiki/Plautus "Plautus"),[[37]](#cite_note-39) [Propertius](/wiki/Propertius "Propertius"),[[38]](#cite_note-40) [Horace](/wiki/Horace "Horace"), [Ovid](/wiki/Ovid "Ovid"), [Martial](/wiki/Martial "Martial") and [Statius](/wiki/Statius "Statius"). The use of Penelope in Latin texts provided a basis for her ongoing use in the Middle Ages and Renaissance as a representation of a chaste wife. This was reinforced by her being named by [Saint Jerome](/wiki/Saint_Jerome "Saint Jerome") among pagan women famed for their chastity.

In [Greek](/wiki/Greek_mythology "Greek mythology") and [Roman mythology](/wiki/Roman_mythology "Roman mythology"), **Odysseus** ([/əˈdɪsiəs/](/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English") [ⓘ](/wiki/File:LL-Q1860_(eng)-Naomi_Persephone_Amethyst_(NaomiAmethyst)-Odysseus_(alt).wav "File:LL-Q1860 (eng)-Naomi Persephone Amethyst (NaomiAmethyst)-Odysseus (alt).wav");[[1]](#cite_note-1) [Ancient Greek](/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ὀδυσσεύς, Ὀδυσεύς, [romanized](/wiki/Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"): *Odysseús, Odyseús*, IPA: [[o.dy(s).sěu̯s]](/wiki/Help:IPA/Greek "Help:IPA/Greek")), also known by the [Latin](/wiki/Latin "Latin") variant **Ulysses** ([/juːˈlɪsiːz/](/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"), [UK](/wiki/British_English "British English") also [/ˈjuːlɪsiːz/](/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [Latin](/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language"): *Ulysses, Ulixes*), is a legendary [Greek](/wiki/Greeks "Greeks") king of [Ithaca](/wiki/Homeric_Ithaca "Homeric Ithaca") and the hero of [Homer](/wiki/Homer "Homer")'s [epic poem](/wiki/Epic_poetry "Epic poetry"), the *[Odyssey](/wiki/Odyssey "Odyssey")*. Odysseus also plays a key role in Homer's *[Iliad](/wiki/Iliad "Iliad")* and other works in that same [epic cycle](/wiki/Epic_cycle "Epic cycle").

As the son of [Laërtes](/wiki/Laertes_(father_of_Odysseus) "Laertes (father of Odysseus)") and [Anticlea](/wiki/Anticlea "Anticlea"), husband of [Penelope](/wiki/Penelope "Penelope"), and father of [Telemachus](/wiki/Telemachus "Telemachus"), Acusilaus, and [Telegonus](/wiki/Telegonus_(son_of_Odysseus) "Telegonus (son of Odysseus)"),[[2]](#cite_note-2) Odysseus is renowned for his intellectual brilliance, guile, and versatility (*polytropos*), and he is thus known by the [epithet](/wiki/Epithet "Epithet") Odysseus the Cunning (Ancient Greek: μῆτις, romanized: *mêtis*, lit. 'cunning intelligence'[[3]](#cite_note-3)). He is most famous for his *[nostos](/wiki/Nostos "Nostos")*, or "homecoming", which took him ten eventful years after the decade-long [Trojan War](/wiki/Trojan_War "Trojan War").[[4]](#cite_note-4)

Name, etymology, and epithets
-----------------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Odysseus&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Name, etymology, and epithets")]

The form Ὀδυσ(σ)εύς *Odys(s)eus* is used starting in the epic period and through the classical period, but various other forms are also found. In vase inscriptions, there are the variants *Oliseus* (Ὀλισεύς), *Olyseus* (Ὀλυσεύς), *Olysseus* (Ὀλυσσεύς), *Olyteus* (Ὀλυτεύς), *Olytteus* (Ὀλυττεύς) and *Ōlysseus* (Ὠλυσσεύς). The form *Oulixēs* (Οὐλίξης) is attested in an early source in [Magna Graecia](/wiki/Magna_Graecia "Magna Graecia") ([Ibycus](/wiki/Ibycus "Ibycus"), according to [Diomedes Grammaticus](/wiki/Diomedes_Grammaticus "Diomedes Grammaticus")), while the Greek grammarian [Aelius Herodianus](/wiki/Aelius_Herodianus "Aelius Herodianus") has *Oulixeus* (Οὐλιξεύς).[[5]](#cite_note-5) In [Latin](/wiki/Latin "Latin"), he was known as **Ulixēs** or (considered less correct) **Ulyssēs**. Some have supposed that "there may originally have been two separate figures, one called something like Odysseus, the other something like Ulixes, who were combined into one complex personality."[[6]](#cite_note-6) However, the change between *d* and *l* is common also in some Indo-European and Greek names,[[7]](#cite_note-7) and the Latin form is supposed to be derived from the [Etruscan](/wiki/Etruscan_language "Etruscan language") **Uthuze** (see below), which perhaps accounts for some of the phonetic innovations.

The etymology of the name is unknown. Ancient authors linked the name to the Greek verbs **odussomai** (ὀδύσσομαι) "to be wroth against, to hate",[[8]](#cite_note-8) to **oduromai** (ὀδύρομαι) "to lament, bewail",[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10) or even to **ollumi** (ὄλλυμι) "to perish, to be lost".[[11]](#cite_note-11)[[12]](#cite_note-Burns2008-12) [Homer](/wiki/Homer "Homer") relates it to various forms of this verb in references and puns. In Book 19 of the *Odyssey*, where Odysseus's early childhood is recounted, [Euryclea](/wiki/Euryclea "Euryclea") asks the boy's grandfather [Autolycus](/wiki/Autolycus "Autolycus") to name him. Euryclea seems to suggest a name like *Polyaretos*, "for he has *much* been *prayed for*" (πολυάρητος) but Autolycus "apparently in a sardonic mood" decided to give the child another name commemorative of "his own experience in life":[[13]](#cite_note-13) "Since I have been angered (ὀδυσσάμενος *odyssamenos*) with many, both men and women, let the name of the child be Odysseus".[[14]](#cite_note-14) Odysseus often receives the [patronymic](/wiki/Patronymic "Patronymic") epithet *Laertiades* (Λαερτιάδης), "son of [Laërtes](/wiki/Laertes_(father_of_Odysseus) "Laertes (father of Odysseus)")".

It has also been suggested that the name is of non-Greek origin, possibly not even [Indo-European](/wiki/Indo-European_languages "Indo-European languages"), with an unknown etymology.[[15]](#cite_note-Dihle1994-15) [Robert S. P. Beekes](/wiki/Robert_S._P._Beekes "Robert S. P. Beekes") has suggested a [Pre-Greek](/wiki/Pre-Greek "Pre-Greek") origin.[[16]](#cite_note-16) In [Etruscan religion](/wiki/Etruscan_religion "Etruscan religion"), the name (and stories) of Odysseus were adopted under the name **Uthuze** (*Uθuze*), which has been interpreted as a parallel borrowing from a preceding [Minoan](/wiki/Minoan_language "Minoan language") form of the name (possibly *\*Oduze*, pronounced [[ˈot͡θut͡se]](/wiki/Help:IPA "Help:IPA")); this theory is also supposed to explain the insecurity of the phonologies (*d* or *l*), since the [affricate](/wiki/Affricate "Affricate") [[t͡θ](/wiki/Voiceless_dental_affricate "Voiceless dental affricate")], unknown to the Greek of that time, gave rise to different counterparts (i. e. *δ* or *λ* in Greek, *θ* in Etruscan).[[17]](#cite_note-17)

In the *Iliad* and *Odyssey,* Homer uses several [epithets](/wiki/Epithets_in_Homer "Epithets in Homer") to describe Odysseus, starting with the opening, where he is described as "the man of many devices" (in the 1919 Murray translation). The Greek word used is *polytropos*, literally the man of many turns, and other translators have suggested alternate English translations, including "man of twists and turns" (Fagles 1996) and "a complicated man" (Wilson 2018).

Description
-----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Odysseus&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Description")]

In the account of [Dares the Phrygian](/wiki/Dares_Phrygius "Dares Phrygius"), Odysseus was illustrated as "tough, crafty, cheerful, of medium height, eloquent, and wise."[[18]](#cite_note-18) In Book III of [Homer](/wiki/Homer "Homer")'s [Iliad](/wiki/Iliad "Iliad"), [Priam](/wiki/Priam "Priam") describes him as "shorter in truth by a head than Atreus' son [Agamemnon](/wiki/Agamemnon "Agamemnon"), / but broader, it would seem, in the chest and across the shoulders /... / Truly, to some deep-fleeced ram would I liken him / who makes his way through the great mass of the shining sheep-flocks."[[19]](#cite_note-19) and in the same book [Antenor](/wiki/Antenor_(Trojan) "Antenor (Trojan)") recalls that "[Menelaus](/wiki/Menelaus "Menelaus") with his broad shoulders was the taller, but Odysseus was the more imposing of the two when they were both seated."[[20]](#cite_note-20) In Book VI of [Homer](/wiki/Homer "Homer")'s [Odyssey](/wiki/Odyssey "Odyssey"), he is described as having "bushy locks" that "hang from his head thick as the petals of a hyacinth in bloom".[[21]](#cite_note-21) In Book XVI of Homer's Odyssey he is said to have a "bronze tan"[[22]](#cite_note-22) and in Book XVIII of Homer's Odyssey, it is said that Odysseus "bared his fine massive thighs. His broad shoulders, his chest and brawny arms were now revealed".[[23]](#cite_note-23)

Genealogy
---------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Odysseus&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Genealogy")]

Relatively little is given of Odysseus's fictional background other than that according to Pseudo-Apollodorus, his paternal grandfather or step-grandfather is [Arcesius](/wiki/Arcesius "Arcesius"), son of [Cephalus](/wiki/Cephalus "Cephalus") and grandson of [Aeolus](/wiki/Aeolus_(son_of_Hellen) "Aeolus (son of Hellen)"), while his maternal grandfather is the thief [Autolycus](/wiki/Autolycus "Autolycus"), son of [Hermes](/wiki/Hermes "Hermes")[[24]](#cite_note-24) and [Chione](/wiki/Chione_(daughter_of_Daedalion) "Chione (daughter of Daedalion)"); this genealogy places Odysseus as the great-grandson of the [Olympian god](/wiki/Twelve_Olympians "Twelve Olympians") Hermes. In the *Odyssey*, however, while Hermes passes on his skill of thievery to Autolycus, there is no indication of a genealogical connection between the two.[[25]](#cite_note-25)[[26]](#cite_note-26)

According to the *Iliad* and *Odyssey*, his father is [Laertes](/wiki/Laertes_(father_of_Odysseus) "Laertes (father of Odysseus)")[[27]](#cite_note-27) and his mother [Anticlea](/wiki/Anticlea "Anticlea"), although there was a non-Homeric tradition[[28]](#cite_note-28)[[29]](#cite_note-29)[[30]](#cite_note-30) that [Sisyphus](/wiki/Sisyphus "Sisyphus") was his true father.[[31]](#cite_note-31) The rumour went that Laërtes bought Odysseus from the conniving king.[[32]](#cite_note-32) Odysseus is said to have a younger sister, [Ctimene](/wiki/Ctimene "Ctimene"), who went to [Same](/wiki/Same_(ancient_Greece) "Same (ancient Greece)") to be married to Eurylochus and is mentioned by the swineherd Eumaeus, whom she grew up alongside, in book 15 of the *Odyssey*.[[33]](#cite_note-Women_in_Odyssey-33)
Odysseus himself, under the guise of an old beggar, gives the swineherd in Ithaca a fictitious genealogy: "From broad Crete I declare that I am come by lineage, the son of a wealthy man. And many other sons too were born and bred in his halls, true sons of a lawful wife; but the mother that bore me was bought, a concubine. Yet [Castor](/wiki/Castor_and_Pollux "Castor and Pollux"), son of [Hylax](/wiki/Hylas "Hylas"), of whom I declare that I am sprung, honored me even as his true-born sons."[[34]](#cite_note-34)

Mythology
---------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Odysseus&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Mythology")]

### Before the Trojan War

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Odysseus&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Before the Trojan War")]

The majority of sources for Odysseus's supposed pre-war exploits—principally the mythographers [Pseudo-Apollodorus](/wiki/Bibliotheca_(Pseudo-Apollodorus) "Bibliotheca (Pseudo-Apollodorus)") and [Hyginus](/wiki/Gaius_Julius_Hyginus "Gaius Julius Hyginus")—postdate Homer by many centuries. Two stories in particular are well known:

When [Helen of Troy](/wiki/Helen_of_Troy "Helen of Troy") is abducted, [Menelaus](/wiki/Menelaus "Menelaus") calls upon the other [suitors](/wiki/Suitors_of_Helen "Suitors of Helen") to honour their oaths and help him to retrieve her, an attempt that leads to the [Trojan War](/wiki/Trojan_War "Trojan War"). Odysseus tries to avoid it by feigning lunacy, as an oracle had prophesied a long-delayed return home for him if he went. He hooks a donkey and an ox to his plow (as they have different stride lengths, hindering the efficiency of the plow) and (some modern sources add) starts [sowing his fields with salt](/wiki/Salting_the_earth "Salting the earth"). [Palamedes](/wiki/Palamedes_(mythology) "Palamedes (mythology)"), at the behest of Menelaus's brother [Agamemnon](/wiki/Agamemnon "Agamemnon"), seeks to disprove Odysseus's madness and places [Telemachus](/wiki/Telemachus "Telemachus"), Odysseus's infant son, in front of the plow. Odysseus veers the plow away from his son, thus exposing his stratagem.[[35]](#cite_note-35) Odysseus holds a grudge against Palamedes during the war for dragging him away from his home.

Odysseus and other envoys of Agamemnon travel to [Scyros](/wiki/Scyros "Scyros") to recruit [Achilles](/wiki/Achilles "Achilles") because of a prophecy that Troy could not be taken without him. By most accounts, [Thetis](/wiki/Thetis "Thetis"), Achilles's mother, disguises him as a woman to hide him from the recruiters because an [oracle](/wiki/Oracle "Oracle") had predicted that Achilles would either live a long uneventful life or achieve everlasting glory while dying young. Odysseus cleverly discovers which among the women before him is Achilles, when Achilles is the only one of them to show interest in examining the weapons hidden among an array of adornment gifts for the daughters of their host. Odysseus arranges further for the sounding of a battle horn, which prompts Achilles to clutch a weapon and show his trained disposition. With his disguise foiled, he is exposed and joins Agamemnon's call to arms among the [Hellenes](/wiki/Hellenes "Hellenes").[[36]](#cite_note-36)

#### The *Iliad*

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Odysseus&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: The Iliad")]

Main article: [Iliad](/wiki/Iliad "Iliad")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9e/Patroclus_corpse_MAN_Firenze.jpg/250px-Patroclus_corpse_MAN_Firenze.jpg)](/wiki/File:Patroclus_corpse_MAN_Firenze.jpg)

[Menelaus](/wiki/Menelaus "Menelaus") and [Meriones](/wiki/Meriones_(mythology) "Meriones (mythology)") lifting [Patroclus](/wiki/Patroclus "Patroclus")'s corpse on a cart while Odysseus looks on, [Etruscan](/wiki/Etruscan_art "Etruscan art") [alabaster](/wiki/Alabaster "Alabaster") urn from [Volterra](/wiki/Volterra "Volterra"), Italy, 2nd century BC

Odysseus is represented as one of the most influential Greek champions during the Trojan War in Homer's account. Along with [Nestor](/wiki/Nestor_(mythology) "Nestor (mythology)") and [Idomeneus](/wiki/Idomeneus "Idomeneus") he is one of the most trusted counsellors and advisors. He always champions the Achaean cause, especially when others question Agamemnon's command, as in one instance when [Thersites](/wiki/Thersites "Thersites") speaks against him. When Agamemnon, to test the morale of the Achaeans, announces his intentions to depart Troy, Odysseus restores order to the Greek camp.[[37]](#cite_note-37) Later on, after many of the heroes leave the battlefield due to injuries (including Odysseus and Agamemnon), Odysseus once again persuades Agamemnon not to withdraw. Along with two other envoys, he is chosen in the failed embassy to try to persuade Achilles to return to combat.[[38]](#cite_note-38)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/Rhesos_MNA_Naples.jpg/250px-Rhesos_MNA_Naples.jpg)](/wiki/File:Rhesos_MNA_Naples.jpg)

Odysseus and [Diomedes](/wiki/Diomedes "Diomedes") stealing the horses of Thracian king [Rhesus](/wiki/Rhesus_of_Thrace "Rhesus of Thrace") they have just killed. Apulian red-figure situla, from Ruvo

When [Hector](/wiki/Hector "Hector") proposes a single combat duel, Odysseus is one of the [Danaans](/wiki/Danaans "Danaans") who reluctantly volunteered to battle him. [Telamonian Ajax](/wiki/Ajax_the_Great "Ajax the Great") ("The Greater"), however, is the volunteer who eventually fights Hector.[[39]](#cite_note-39) Odysseus aids [Diomedes](/wiki/Diomedes "Diomedes") during the night operations to kill [Rhesus](/wiki/Rhesus_of_Thrace "Rhesus of Thrace"), because it had been foretold that if his horses drank from the [Scamander River](/wiki/Karamenderes_River "Karamenderes River"), Troy could not be taken.[[40]](#cite_note-40)

After [Patroclus](/wiki/Patroclus "Patroclus") is slain, it is Odysseus who counsels Achilles to let the [Achaean](/wiki/Achaea_(ancient_region) "Achaea (ancient region)") men eat and rest rather than follow his rage-driven desire to go back on the offensive—and kill Trojans—immediately. Eventually (and reluctantly), he consents.[[41]](#cite_note-41) During the funeral games for Patroclus, Odysseus becomes involved in a wrestling match with Ajax "The Greater" and foot race with Ajax "The Lesser", son of Oileus and Nestor's son [Antilochus](/wiki/Antilochus "Antilochus"). He draws the wrestling match, and with the help of the goddess [Athena](/wiki/Athena "Athena"), he wins the race.[[42]](#cite_note-42)

Odysseus has traditionally been viewed as Achilles's antithesis in the *Iliad*:[[43]](#cite_note-43) while Achilles's anger is all-consuming and of a self-destructive nature, Odysseus is frequently viewed as a man of the mean, a voice of reason, renowned for his self-restraint and diplomatic skills. He is also in some respects antithetical to Telamonian Ajax (Shakespeare's "beef-witted" Ajax): while the latter has only brawn to recommend him, Odysseus is not only ingenious (as evidenced by his idea for the Trojan Horse), but an eloquent speaker, a skill perhaps best demonstrated in the embassy to Achilles in book 9 of the *Iliad*. The two are not only foils in the abstract but often opposed in practice since they have many duels and run-ins.

#### Other stories from the Trojan War

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Odysseus&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Other stories from the Trojan War")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/05-Mosaico_del_Oecus._Aquiles_en_Skyros_alta.jpg/250px-05-Mosaico_del_Oecus._Aquiles_en_Skyros_alta.jpg)](/wiki/File:05-Mosaico_del_Oecus._Aquiles_en_Skyros_alta.jpg)

[Roman mosaic](/wiki/Roman_mosaic "Roman mosaic") depicting Odysseus at Skyros unveiling the disguised [Achilles](/wiki/Achilles "Achilles");[[44]](#cite_note-44) from [La Olmeda](/wiki/La_Olmeda "La Olmeda"), [Pedrosa de la Vega](/wiki/Pedrosa_de_la_Vega "Pedrosa de la Vega"), Spain, 5th century AD

Since a prophecy suggested that the Trojan War would not be won without [Achilles](/wiki/Achilles "Achilles"), Odysseus and several other [Achaean](/wiki/Achaeans_(Homer) "Achaeans (Homer)") leaders are described in the *[Achilleid](/wiki/Achilleid "Achilleid")* as having gone to [Skyros](/wiki/Achilles_on_Skyros "Achilles on Skyros") to find him. Odysseus discovered Achilles by offering gifts, adornments and musical instruments as well as weapons, to the king's daughters, and then having his companions imitate the noises of an enemy's attack on the island (most notably, making a blast of a trumpet heard), which prompted Achilles to reveal himself by picking a weapon to fight back, and together they departed for the Trojan War.[[45]](#cite_note-45)

The story of the death of [Palamedes](/wiki/Palamedes_(mythology) "Palamedes (mythology)") has many versions. According to some, Odysseus never forgives Palamedes for unmasking his [feigned madness](/wiki/Feigned_madness "Feigned madness") and plays a part in his downfall. One tradition says Odysseus convinces a Trojan captive to write a letter pretending to be from Palamedes. A sum of gold is mentioned to have been sent as a reward for Palamedes's treachery. Odysseus then kills the prisoner and hides the gold in Palamedes's tent. He ensures that the letter is found and acquired by Agamemnon, and also gives hints directing the Argives to the gold. This is evidence enough for the Greeks, and they have Palamedes stoned to death. Other sources say that Odysseus and Diomedes goad Palamedes into descending a well with the prospect of treasure being at the bottom. When Palamedes reaches the bottom, the two proceed to bury him with stones, killing him.[[46]](#cite_note-46)

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Odysseus_Ajax_Louvre_F340.jpg/250px-Odysseus_Ajax_Louvre_F340.jpg)](/wiki/File:Odysseus_Ajax_Louvre_F340.jpg)

Oinochoe, *ca* 520 BC, Odysseus and [Ajax](/wiki/Ajax_the_Great "Ajax the Great") fighting over the armour of Achilles

When Achilles is slain in battle by [Paris](/wiki/Paris_(mythology) "Paris (mythology)"), it is Odysseus and [Ajax](/wiki/Ajax_the_Great "Ajax the Great") who retrieve the fallen warrior's body and armour in the thick of heavy fighting. During the funeral games for Achilles, Odysseus competes once again with Ajax. Thetis says that the arms of Achilles will go to the bravest of the Greeks, but only these two warriors dare lay claim to that title. The two Argives became embroiled in a heavy dispute about one another's merits to receive the reward. The Greeks dither out of fear in deciding a winner, because they did not want to insult one and have him abandon the war effort. [Nestor](/wiki/Nestor_(mythology) "Nestor (mythology)") suggests that they allow the captive Trojans to decide the winner.[[47]](#cite_note-47) The accounts of the *Odyssey* disagree, suggesting that the Greeks themselves hold a secret vote.[[48]](#cite_note-48) In any case, Odysseus is the winner. Enraged and humiliated, Ajax is driven mad by Athena. When he returns to his senses, in shame at how he has slaughtered livestock in his madness, Ajax kills himself by the sword that Hector had given him after their duel.[[49]](#cite_note-49)

Together with Diomedes, Odysseus fetches Achilles's son, [Pyrrhus](/wiki/Neoptolemus "Neoptolemus"), to come to the aid of the Achaeans, because an oracle had stated that Troy could not be taken without him. A great warrior, Pyrrhus is also called Neoptolemus (Greek for "new warrior"). Upon the success of the mission, Odysseus gives Achilles's armour to him.

It is learned that the war can not be won without the poisonous arrows of [Heracles](/wiki/Heracles "Heracles"), which are owned by the abandoned [Philoctetes](/wiki/Philoctetes "Philoctetes"). Odysseus and Diomedes (or, according to some accounts, Odysseus and [Neoptolemus](/wiki/Neoptolemus "Neoptolemus")) leave to retrieve them. Upon their arrival, Philoctetes (still suffering from the wound) is seen still to be enraged at the [Danaans](/wiki/Danaans "Danaans"), especially at Odysseus, for abandoning him. Although his first instinct is to shoot Odysseus, his anger is eventually defused by Odysseus's persuasive powers and the influence of the gods. Odysseus returns to the Argive camp with Philoctetes and his arrows.[[50]](#cite_note-50)

Perhaps Odysseus's most famous contribution to the Greek war effort is devising the strategy of the [Trojan Horse](/wiki/Trojan_Horse "Trojan Horse"), which allows the Greek army to sneak into Troy under cover of darkness. It is built by [Epeius](/wiki/Epeius_of_Phocis "Epeius of Phocis") and filled with Greek warriors, led by Odysseus.[[51]](#cite_note-51) Odysseus and Diomedes steal the [Palladium](/wiki/Palladium_(mythology) "Palladium (mythology)") that lay within Troy's walls, for the Greeks were told they could not sack the city without it. Some late Roman sources indicate that Odysseus schemed to kill his partner on the way back, but Diomedes thwarts this attempt.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/32/Wall_painting_-_rape_of_the_palladion_-_Pompeii_%28I_2_26%29_-_Napoli_MAN_109751_-_02.jpg/250px-Wall_painting_-_rape_of_the_palladion_-_Pompeii_%28I_2_26%29_-_Napoli_MAN_109751_-_02.jpg)](/wiki/File:Wall_painting_-_rape_of_the_palladion_-_Pompeii_(I_2_26)_-_Napoli_MAN_109751_-_02.jpg)

Odysseus ([pileus hat](/wiki/Pileus_(hat) "Pileus (hat)")) carrying off the [palladion](/wiki/Palladion "Palladion") from [Troy](/wiki/Troy "Troy"), with the help of [Diomedes](/wiki/Diomedes "Diomedes"), against the resistance of [Cassandra](/wiki/Cassandra "Cassandra") and other Trojans. #### "Cruel, deceitful Ulixes" of the Romans

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Odysseus&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: \"Cruel, deceitful Ulixes\" of the Romans")]

Homer's *Iliad* and *Odyssey* portray Odysseus as a [culture hero](/wiki/Culture_hero "Culture hero"), but the Romans, who believed themselves the heirs of Prince [Aeneas](/wiki/Aeneas "Aeneas") of Troy, considered him a villainous falsifier. In [Virgil](/wiki/Virgil "Virgil")'s *[Aeneid](/wiki/Aeneid "Aeneid")*, written between 29 and 19 BC, he is constantly referred to as "cruel Odysseus" ([Latin](/wiki/Latin "Latin") *dirus Ulixes*) or "deceitful Odysseus" (*pellacis*, *fandi fictor*). Turnus, in *Aeneid*, book 9, reproaches the Trojan Ascanius with images of rugged, forthright Latin virtues, declaring (in [John Dryden](/wiki/John_Dryden "John Dryden")'s translation), "You shall not find the sons of Atreus here, nor need the frauds of sly Ulysses fear." While the Greeks admired his cunning and deceit, these qualities did not recommend themselves to the Romans, who possessed a rigid sense of honour. In Euripides's tragedy *[Iphigenia at Aulis](/wiki/Iphigenia_at_Aulis "Iphigenia at Aulis")*, having convinced Agamemnon to consent to the sacrifice of his daughter, Iphigenia, to appease the goddess [Artemis](/wiki/Artemis "Artemis"), Odysseus facilitates the immolation by telling Iphigenia's mother, [Clytemnestra](/wiki/Clytemnestra "Clytemnestra"), that the girl is to be wed to [Achilles](/wiki/Achilles "Achilles"). Odysseus's attempts to avoid his sacred oath to defend [Menelaus](/wiki/Menelaus "Menelaus") and [Helen](/wiki/Helen_of_Troy "Helen of Troy") offended Roman notions of duty, and the many stratagems and tricks that he employed to get his way offended Roman notions of honour.

### Journey home to Ithaca

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Odysseus&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Journey home to Ithaca")]

Further information: [Homer's Ithaca](/wiki/Homer%27s_Ithaca "Homer's Ithaca") and [Returns from Troy](/wiki/Returns_from_Troy "Returns from Troy")

Odysseus is probably best known as the eponymous hero of the *Odyssey*. This epic describes his travels, which lasted for 10 years, as he tries to return home after the Trojan War and reassert his place as rightful king of Ithaca.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/Arnold_B%C3%B6cklin_-_Odysseus_and_Polyphemus.jpg/250px-Arnold_B%C3%B6cklin_-_Odysseus_and_Polyphemus.jpg)](/wiki/File:Arnold_B%C3%B6cklin_-_Odysseus_and_Polyphemus.jpg)

*[Odysseus and Polyphemus](/wiki/Odysseus_and_Polyphemus_(B%C3%B6cklin) "Odysseus and Polyphemus (Böcklin)")* (1896) by [Arnold Böcklin](/wiki/Arnold_B%C3%B6cklin "Arnold Böcklin"): Odysseus and his crew escape the Cyclops [Polyphemus](/wiki/Polyphemus "Polyphemus").

Homebound from Troy, after a raid on [Ismarus](/wiki/Ismara "Ismara") in the land of the [Cicones](/wiki/Cicones "Cicones"), he and his twelve ships are driven off course by storms. They visit the lethargic [Lotus-Eaters](/wiki/Lotus-eaters "Lotus-eaters") and are captured by the [Cyclops](/wiki/Cyclopes "Cyclopes") [Polyphemus](/wiki/Polyphemus "Polyphemus") while visiting his island. After Polyphemus eats several of his men, he and Odysseus have a discussion and Odysseus tells Polyphemus his name is [Outis](/wiki/Outis "Outis") ("Nobody"). Odysseus takes a barrel of wine and the Cyclops drinks it, falling asleep. Odysseus and his men take a wooden stake, ignite it with the remaining wine, and blind him. While they escape, Polyphemus cries in pain, and the other Cyclopes ask him what is wrong. Polyphemus cries, "Nobody has blinded me!" and the other Cyclopes think he has gone mad. Odysseus and his crew escape, but Odysseus rashly reveals his real name, and Polyphemus prays to Poseidon, his father, to take revenge. They stay with [Aeolus](/wiki/Aeolus_(son_of_Hippotes) "Aeolus (son of Hippotes)"), the master of the winds, who gives Odysseus a leather bag containing all the winds, except the west wind, a gift that should have ensured a safe return home. However, the sailors foolishly open the bag while Odysseus sleeps, thinking that it contains gold. All of the winds fly out, and the resulting storm drives the ships back the way they had come, just as Ithaca comes into sight.[[52]](#cite_note-52)

After pleading in vain with Aeolus to help them again, they re-embark and encounter the cannibalistic [Laestrygonians](/wiki/Laestrygonians "Laestrygonians"). Odysseus's ship is the only one to escape. He sails on and visits the witch-goddess [Circe](/wiki/Circe "Circe"). She turns half of his men into swine after feeding them cheese and wine. Hermes warns Odysseus about Circe and gives him a drug called [moly](/wiki/Moly_(herb) "Moly (herb)"), which resists Circe's magic. Circe, being attracted to Odysseus's resistance, falls in love with him and releases his men. Odysseus and his crew remain with her on the island for one year, while they feast and drink. Finally, Odysseus's men convince him to leave for Ithaca.

Guided by Circe's instructions, Odysseus and his crew cross the ocean and reach a harbor at the western edge of the world, where Odysseus sacrifices to the dead and [summons the spirit](/wiki/Nekuia "Nekuia") of the old prophet [Tiresias](/wiki/Tiresias "Tiresias") for advice. Next Odysseus meets the spirit of his own mother, who had died of grief during his long absence. From her, he learns for the first time news of his own household, threatened by the greed of [Penelope](/wiki/Penelope "Penelope")'s [suitors](/wiki/Suitors_of_Penelope "Suitors of Penelope"). Odysseus also talks to his fallen war comrades and the mortal shade of [Heracles](/wiki/Heracles "Heracles").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Mosa%C3%AFque_d%27Ulysse_et_les_sir%C3%A8nes.jpg/250px-Mosa%C3%AFque_d%27Ulysse_et_les_sir%C3%A8nes.jpg)](/wiki/File:Mosa%C3%AFque_d%27Ulysse_et_les_sir%C3%A8nes.jpg)

Odysseus and the [Sirens](/wiki/Siren_(mythology) "Siren (mythology)"), Ulixes [mosaic](/wiki/Mosaic "Mosaic") at the [Bardo National Museum](/wiki/Bardo_National_Museum_(Tunis) "Bardo National Museum (Tunis)") in [Tunis](/wiki/Tunis "Tunis"), Tunisia, 2nd century AD

Odysseus and his men return to Circe's island, and she advises them on the remaining stages of the journey. They skirt the land of the [Sirens](/wiki/Siren_(mythology) "Siren (mythology)"), pass between the six-headed monster [Scylla](/wiki/Scylla "Scylla") and the whirlpool [Charybdis](/wiki/Charybdis "Charybdis"), where they row directly between the two. However, [Scylla](/wiki/Scylla "Scylla") drags the boat towards her by grabbing the oars and eats six men.

They land on the island of [Thrinacia](/wiki/Thrinacia "Thrinacia"). There, Odysseus's men ignore the warnings of Tiresias and Circe and hunt down the sacred cattle of the sun god [Helios](/wiki/Helios "Helios"). Helios tells [Zeus](/wiki/Zeus "Zeus") what happened and demands Odysseus's men be punished or else he will take the sun and shine it in the Underworld. Zeus fulfills Helios's demands by causing a shipwreck during a thunderstorm in which all but Odysseus drown. He washes ashore on the island of [Ogygia](/wiki/Ogygia "Ogygia"), where [Calypso](/wiki/Calypso_(mythology) "Calypso (mythology)") compels him to remain as her lover for seven years. He finally escapes when [Hermes](/wiki/Hermes "Hermes") tells Calypso to release Odysseus.[[53]](#cite_note-53)

Odysseus is shipwrecked and befriended by the [Phaeacians](/wiki/Scheria "Scheria"). After he tells them his story, the Phaeacians, led by King [Alcinous](/wiki/Alcinous "Alcinous"), agree to help Odysseus get home. They deliver him at night, while he is fast asleep, to a hidden harbor on Ithaca. He finds his way to the hut of one of his own former slaves, the swineherd [Eumaeus](/wiki/Eumaeus "Eumaeus"), and also meets up with his son [Telemachus](/wiki/Telemachus "Telemachus") returning from Sparta. Athena disguises Odysseus as a wandering beggar to learn how things stand in his household.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3c/The_return_of_Ulysses.gif/250px-The_return_of_Ulysses.gif)](/wiki/File:The_return_of_Ulysses.gif)

The return of Ulysses, illustration by E. M. Synge from the 1909 *Story of the World* children's book series (book 1: *On the shores of Great Sea*)

When the disguised Odysseus returns after 20 years, he is recognized only by his faithful dog, [Argos](/wiki/Argos_(dog) "Argos (dog)"). Penelope announces in her long interview with the disguised hero that whoever can string Odysseus's rigid bow and shoot an arrow through twelve axe shafts may have her hand. According to [Bernard Knox](/wiki/Bernard_Knox "Bernard Knox"), "For the plot of the *Odyssey*, of course, her decision is the turning point, the move that makes possible the long-predicted triumph of the returning hero".[[54]](#cite_note-54) Odysseus's identity is discovered by the housekeeper, [Eurycleia](/wiki/Eurycleia "Eurycleia"), as she is washing his feet and discovers an old scar Odysseus received during a boar hunt. Odysseus swears her to secrecy, threatening to kill her if she tells anyone.

When the contest of the bow begins, none of the suitors are able to string the bow. After all the suitors have given up, the disguised Odysseus asks to participate. Though the suitors refuse at first, Penelope intervenes and allows the "stranger" (the disguised Odysseus) to participate. Odysseus easily strings his bow and wins the contest. Having done so, he proceeds to slaughter the suitors (beginning with Antinous whom he finds drinking from Odysseus's cup) with help from Telemachus and two of Odysseus's servants, [Eumaeus](/wiki/Eumaeus "Eumaeus") the swineherd and [Philoetius](/wiki/Philoetius "Philoetius") the cowherd. Odysseus tells the serving women who slept with the suitors to clean up the mess of corpses and then has those women hanged in terror. He tells Telemachus that he will replenish his stocks by raiding nearby islands. Odysseus has now revealed himself in all his glory (with a little makeover by Athena); yet Penelope cannot believe that her husband has really returned—she fears that it is perhaps some god in disguise, as in the story of [Alcmene](/wiki/Alcmene "Alcmene") (mother of Heracles)—and tests him by ordering her servant Euryclea to move the bed in their wedding-chamber. Odysseus protests that this cannot be done since he made the bed himself and knows that one of its legs is a living [olive tree](/wiki/Olive_tree "Olive tree"). Penelope finally accepts that he truly is her husband, a moment that highlights their *homophrosýnē* ("like-mindedness").

The next day Odysseus and Telemachus visit the country farm of his old father [Laërtes](/wiki/Laertes_(father_of_Odysseus) "Laertes (father of Odysseus)"). The citizens of Ithaca follow Odysseus on the road, planning to avenge the killing of the Suitors, their sons. The goddess Athena and the god Zeus intervene and persuade both sides to make peace.[[55]](#cite_note-55)

### Other tales

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Odysseus&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Other tales")]

According to some late sources, most of them purely genealogical, Odysseus had many other children besides [Telemachus](/wiki/Telemachus "Telemachus"). Most such genealogies aimed to link Odysseus with the foundation of many [Italic](/wiki/Italy "Italy") cities.[[56]](#cite_note-56) This would seem to contradict *The Odyssey*, which says that Odysseus's family line can only produce a single child per generation by the order of Zeus, with Telemachus already existing as that sole heir.[[57]](#cite_note-After_the_Odyssey-57)[[58]](#cite_note-58) However, the *Odyssey* also notes the existence of Odysseus's sister, Ctimene.[[33]](#cite_note-Women_in_Odyssey-33)

The most famous of the other children are:

* with [Penelope](/wiki/Penelope "Penelope"): [Poliporthes](/wiki/Poliporthes "Poliporthes") (born after Odysseus's return from Troy)
* with [Circe](/wiki/Circe "Circe"): [Telegonus](/wiki/Telegonus_(son_of_Odysseus) "Telegonus (son of Odysseus)"), [Ardeas](/wiki/Ardeas "Ardeas"), [Latinus](/wiki/Latinus "Latinus"), also [Auson](/wiki/Auson_(king) "Auson (king)") and [Cassiphone](/wiki/Cassiphone "Cassiphone").[[59]](#cite_note-59) [Xenagoras](/wiki/Xenagoras_(historian) "Xenagoras (historian)") writes that Odysseus with Circe had three sons, [Romos](/wiki/Rhomos "Rhomos") ([Ancient Greek](/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ῥώμος), [Anteias](/wiki/Anteias "Anteias") ([Ancient Greek](/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀντείας) and [Ardeias](/wiki/Ardeias "Ardeias") ([Ancient Greek](/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἀρδείας), who built three cities and called them after their own names. The city that Romos founded was [Rome](/wiki/Rome "Rome").[[60]](#cite_note-60)
* with [Calypso](/wiki/Calypso_(mythology) "Calypso (mythology)"): [Nausithous](/wiki/Nausithous "Nausithous"), [Nausinous](/wiki/Nausinous "Nausinous")
* with [Callidice](/wiki/Callidice_of_Thesprotia "Callidice of Thesprotia"): [Polypoetes](/wiki/Polypoetes "Polypoetes")
* with [Euippe](/wiki/Euippe_(daughter_of_Tyrimmas) "Euippe (daughter of Tyrimmas)"): [Euryalus](/wiki/Euryalus "Euryalus")
* with daughter of [Thoas](/wiki/Thoas_(king_of_Aetoila) "Thoas (king of Aetoila)"): Leontophonus

He figures in the end of the story of King [Telephus](/wiki/Telephus "Telephus") of [Mysia](/wiki/Mysia "Mysia").

The last poem in the [Epic Cycle](/wiki/Epic_Cycle "Epic Cycle") is called the *[Telegony](/wiki/Telegony "Telegony")*, and is now lost. According to remaining fragments, it told the story of Odysseus's last voyage to the land of the Thesprotians. There he married the queen [Callidice](/wiki/Callidice_of_Thesprotia "Callidice of Thesprotia"). Then he led the Thesprotians in a war with their neighbors the Brygoi (Brygi, Brygians) and defeated in battle the neighboring peoples who attacked him. When Callidice died, Odysseus returned home to Ithaca, leaving their son, [Polypoetes](/wiki/Polypoetes "Polypoetes"), to rule Thesprotia.[[61]](#cite_note-CinaethonTelegony-61) Contradicting the reading of Tiresias's prophecy in *The Odyssey* that Odysseus will have a gentle death in old age after making it home,[[57]](#cite_note-After_the_Odyssey-57)[[62]](#cite_note-62) the *Telogony* claims that he met his death at the hands of [Telegonus](/wiki/Telegonus_(son_of_Odysseus) "Telegonus (son of Odysseus)"), his son with Circe, after a misunderstanding. Telegonus attacked his father with a poisoned, stingray spine-tipped spear, given to him by Circe. Before dying, Odysseus recognized his son. Telegonus then brought back his father's corpse to Aeaea, together with Penelope and Odysseus's son by her, Telemachus. After burying Odysseus, Circe made the other three immortal. Circe married Telemachus, and Telegonus married Penelope[[61]](#cite_note-CinaethonTelegony-61) by the advice of Athena.[[63]](#cite_note-63) An alternative version to Odysseus' death by stingray spine was presented in the *Ghost-Raisers*, a lost fifth-century BC tragedy by [Aeschylus](/wiki/Aeschylus "Aeschylus") inspired by the nekyia episode of the *Odyssey*. In the tragedy, the dead Tiresias predicted that one day a heron's droppings containing said barb would fall upon an aged Odysseus' bald head and rot his skin.[[64]](#cite_note-64)

According to what seems to be later tradition, Odysseus was resurrected by Circe after his death at the hands of Telegonus. Afterward, he married Telemachus to [Cassiphone](/wiki/Cassiphone "Cassiphone"), the daughter he had with Circe.[[65]](#cite_note-65)[[66]](#cite_note-66) Telemachus however killed Circe after a quarrel, causing Cassiphone to kill him in revenge. Odysseus witnessing those unfortunate events died again, of grief this time.[[67]](#cite_note-67)

In 5th century BC [Athens](/wiki/Athens "Athens"), tales of the Trojan War were popular subjects for [tragedies](/wiki/Tragedies "Tragedies"). Odysseus figures centrally or indirectly in a number of the extant plays by [Aeschylus](/wiki/Aeschylus "Aeschylus"), [Sophocles](/wiki/Sophocles "Sophocles") (*[Ajax](/wiki/Ajax_(Sophocles) "Ajax (Sophocles)")*, *[Philoctetes](/wiki/Philoctetes_(Sophocles) "Philoctetes (Sophocles)")*) and [Euripides](/wiki/Euripides "Euripides") (*[Hecuba](/wiki/Hecuba_(play) "Hecuba (play)")*, *[Rhesus](/wiki/Rhesus_(play) "Rhesus (play)")*, *[Cyclops](/wiki/Cyclops_(play) "Cyclops (play)")*) and figured in still more that have not survived. In his *Ajax*, Sophocles portrays Odysseus as a modern voice of reasoning compared to the title character's rigid antiquity.

[Plato](/wiki/Plato "Plato") in his dialogue *[Hippias Minor](/wiki/Hippias_Minor "Hippias Minor")* examines a literary question about whom Homer intended to portray as the better man, Achilles or Odysseus.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/92/Odysseus_-01.jpg/330px-Odysseus_-01.jpg)](/wiki/File:Odysseus_-01.jpg)

Head of Odysseus wearing a [pileus](/wiki/Pileus_(hat) "Pileus (hat)") depicted on a 3rd-century BC coin from [Ithaca](/wiki/Ithaca_(island) "Ithaca (island)")

[Pausanias](/wiki/Pausanias_(geographer) "Pausanias (geographer)") at the *[Description of Greece](/wiki/Description_of_Greece "Description of Greece")* writes that at [Pheneus](/wiki/Pheneus "Pheneus") there was a bronze statue of Poseidon, surnamed Hippios ([Ancient Greek](/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ἵππιος), meaning *of horse*, which according to the legends was dedicated by Odysseus and also a sanctuary of [Artemis](/wiki/Artemis "Artemis") which was called Heurippa ([Ancient Greek](/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Εὑρίππα), meaning *horse finder*, and was founded by Odysseus.[[68]](#cite_note-perseus.tufts.edu-68) According to the legends Odysseus lost his mares and traversed Greece in search of them. He found them on that site in Pheneus.[[68]](#cite_note-perseus.tufts.edu-68) Pausanias adds that according to the people of Pheneus, when Odysseus found his mares he decided to keep horses in the land of Pheneus, just as he reared his cows. The people of Pheneus also pointed out to him writing, purporting to be instructions of Odysseus to those tending his mares.[[69]](#cite_note-69)

As Ulysses, he is mentioned regularly in [Virgil](/wiki/Virgil "Virgil")'s *[Aeneid](/wiki/Aeneid "Aeneid")* written between 29 and 19 BC, and the poem's hero, [Aeneas](/wiki/Aeneas "Aeneas"), rescues one of Ulysses's crew members who was left behind on the island of the Cyclopes. He in turn offers a first-person account of some of the same events Homer relates, in which Ulysses appears directly. Virgil's Ulysses typifies his view of the Greeks: he is cunning but impious, and ultimately malicious and hedonistic.

[Ovid](/wiki/Ovid "Ovid") retells parts of Ulysses's journeys, focusing on his romantic involvements with Circe and Calypso, and recasts him as, in [Harold Bloom](/wiki/Harold_Bloom "Harold Bloom")'s phrase, "one of the great wandering womanizers". Ovid also gives a detailed account of the contest between Ulysses and [Ajax](/wiki/Ajax_the_Great "Ajax the Great") for the armour of Achilles.

Greek legend tells of Ulysses as the founder of [Lisbon](/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon"), Portugal, calling it *Ulisipo* or *Ulisseya*, during his twenty-year errand on the Mediterranean and Atlantic seas.[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] [Olisipo](/wiki/Olisipo "Olisipo") was Lisbon's name in the Roman Empire. This [folk etymology](/wiki/Folk_etymology "Folk etymology") is recounted by [Strabo](/wiki/Strabo "Strabo") based on [Asclepiades of Myrlea](/wiki/Asclepiades_of_Myrlea "Asclepiades of Myrlea")'s words,[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] by [Pomponius Mela](/wiki/Pomponius_Mela "Pomponius Mela"),[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] by [Gaius Julius Solinus](/wiki/Gaius_Julius_Solinus "Gaius Julius Solinus") (3rd century AD)[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*], and would later be reiterated by [Camões](/wiki/Lu%C3%ADs_de_Cam%C3%B5es "Luís de Camões") in his epic poem *[Os Lusíadas](/wiki/Os_Lus%C3%ADadas "Os Lusíadas")* (first printed in 1572).[*[citation needed](/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

In one version of Odysseus's end, he is eventually turned into a horse by Athena.[[70]](#cite_note-70)

In post-classical tradition
---------------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Odysseus&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: In post-classical tradition")]

Odysseus is one of the most recurrent characters in [Western culture](/wiki/Western_culture "Western culture").

### Middle Ages and Renaissance

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Odysseus&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Middle Ages and Renaissance")]

[Dante Alighieri](/wiki/Dante_Alighieri "Dante Alighieri"), in the [Canto](/wiki/Canto "Canto") XXVI of the *[Inferno](/wiki/Inferno_(Dante) "Inferno (Dante)")* segment of his *[Divine Comedy](/wiki/Divine_Comedy "Divine Comedy")* (1308–1320), encounters Odysseus ("Ulisse" in Italian) near the very bottom of Hell: with [Diomedes](/wiki/Diomedes "Diomedes"), he walks wrapped in flame in the eighth ring (*Counselors of Fraud*) of the [Eighth Circle](/wiki/Malebolge "Malebolge") (*Sins of Malice*), as punishment for his schemes and conspiracies that won the Trojan War. In a famous passage, Dante has Odysseus relate a different version of his voyage and death from the one told by Homer. He tells how he set out with his men from Circe's island for a journey of exploration to sail beyond the [Pillars of Hercules](/wiki/Pillars_of_Hercules "Pillars of Hercules") and into the Western sea to find what adventures awaited them. Men, says Ulisse, are not made to live like brutes, but to follow virtue and knowledge.[[71]](#cite_note-71)

After travelling west and south for five months, they see in the distance a great mountain rising from the sea (this is [Purgatory](/wiki/Purgatory "Purgatory"), in Dante's cosmology) before a storm sinks them. Dante did not have access to the original Greek texts of the Homeric epics, so his knowledge of their subject-matter was based only on information from later sources, chiefly [Virgil](/wiki/Virgil "Virgil")'s *[Aeneid](/wiki/Aeneid "Aeneid")* but also [Ovid](/wiki/Ovid "Ovid"); hence the discrepancy between Dante and Homer.[[72]](#cite_note-72)

He appears in [Shakespeare](/wiki/Shakespeare "Shakespeare")'s *[Troilus and Cressida](/wiki/Troilus_and_Cressida "Troilus and Cressida")* (1602), set during the Trojan War.

### Modern literature

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Odysseus&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Modern literature")]

#### Poetry

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Odysseus&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Poetry")]

In her poem [![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Wikisource-logo.svg/20px-Wikisource-logo.svg.png)](/wiki/File:Wikisource-logo.svg) [Site of the Castle of Ulysses](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Letitia_Elizabeth_Landon_(L._E._L.)_in_Fisher%27s_Drawing_Room_Scrap_Book,_1837/Site_of_the_Castle_of_Ulysses "s:Letitia Elizabeth Landon (L. E. L.) in Fisher's Drawing Room Scrap Book, 1837/Site of the Castle of Ulysses"). (published in 1836), [Letitia Elizabeth Landon](/wiki/Letitia_Elizabeth_Landon "Letitia Elizabeth Landon") gives her version of *The Song of the Sirens* with an explanation of its purpose, structure and meaning. This illustrates a painting by [Charles Bentley](/wiki/Charles_Bentley_(painter) "Charles Bentley (painter)") engraved by R. Sands, and showing The Black Mountains of [Cephalonia](/wiki/Cephalonia "Cephalonia") in the background.[[73]](#cite_note-73) A further poetical illustration, also in Fisher's Drawing Room Scrap Book, 1837, is to an engraving of a painting by [Charles Bentley](/wiki/Charles_Bentley_(painter) "Charles Bentley (painter)"), [![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4c/Wikisource-logo.svg/20px-Wikisource-logo.svg.png)](/wiki/File:Wikisource-logo.svg) [Town and Harbour of Ithaca](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Letitia_Elizabeth_Landon_(L._E._L.)_in_Fisher%27s_Drawing_Room_Scrap_Book,_1837/Town_and_Harbour_of_Ithaca "s:Letitia Elizabeth Landon (L. E. L.) in Fisher's Drawing Room Scrap Book, 1837/Town and Harbour of Ithaca"). and harks back to the island 'where Ulysses was king'.[[74]](#cite_note-74)

[Alfred, Lord Tennyson](/wiki/Alfred,_Lord_Tennyson "Alfred, Lord Tennyson")'s poem "[Ulysses](/wiki/Ulysses_(poem) "Ulysses (poem)")" (published in 1842) presents an aging king who has seen too much of the world to be happy sitting on a throne idling his days away. Leaving the task of civilizing his people to his son, he gathers together a band of old comrades "to sail beyond the sunset".

[Nikos Kazantzakis](/wiki/Nikos_Kazantzakis "Nikos Kazantzakis")'s *[The Odyssey: A Modern Sequel](/wiki/The_Odyssey:_A_Modern_Sequel "The Odyssey: A Modern Sequel")* (1938), a 33,333-line epic poem, begins with Odysseus cleansing his body of the blood of [Penelope](/wiki/Penelope "Penelope")'s suitors. Odysseus soon leaves Ithaca in search of new adventures. Before his death he abducts Helen, incites revolutions in [Crete](/wiki/Crete "Crete") and [Egypt](/wiki/Egypt "Egypt"), communes with God, and meets representatives of such famous historical and literary figures as [Lenin](/wiki/Lenin "Lenin"), [Don Quixote](/wiki/Alonso_Quijano "Alonso Quijano") and [Jesus](/wiki/Jesus_Christ "Jesus Christ").

In 1986, Irish poet [Eilean Ni Chuilleanain](/wiki/Eilean_Ni_Chuilleanain "Eilean Ni Chuilleanain") published "The Second Voyage", a poem in which she makes use of the story of Odysseus.

#### Novels

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Odysseus&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Novels")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5f/Bay_of_Palaiokastritsa_from_Bellavista.JPG/250px-Bay_of_Palaiokastritsa_from_Bellavista.JPG)](/wiki/File:Bay_of_Palaiokastritsa_from_Bellavista.JPG)

The bay of [Palaiokastritsa](/wiki/Palaiokastritsa "Palaiokastritsa") in [Corfu](/wiki/Corfu "Corfu") as seen from Bella vista of Lakones, considered to be the place where Odysseus disembarked and met [Nausicaa](/wiki/Nausicaa "Nausicaa") for the first time. The rock in the sea near the horizon at the top centre-left is held by the locals to be the mythical petrified ship of Odysseus.

[Frederick Rolfe](/wiki/Frederick_Rolfe "Frederick Rolfe")'s *The Weird of the Wanderer* (1912) has the hero Nicholas Crabbe (based on the author) travelling back in time, discovering that he is the reincarnation of Odysseus, marrying Helen, being deified and ending up as one of the three [Magi](/wiki/Biblical_Magi "Biblical Magi").

[James Joyce](/wiki/James_Joyce "James Joyce")'s novel *[Ulysses](/wiki/Ulysses_(novel) "Ulysses (novel)")* (first published 1918–1920) uses modern literary devices to narrate a single day in the life of a Dublin businessman named [Leopold Bloom](/wiki/Leopold_Bloom "Leopold Bloom"). Bloom's day bears many elaborate parallels to Odysseus's ten years of wandering.

*[Return to Ithaca](/wiki/Return_to_Ithaca_(novel) "Return to Ithaca (novel)")* (1946) by [Eyvind Johnson](/wiki/Eyvind_Johnson "Eyvind Johnson") is a retelling of the events that adds a psychological study of the characters of Odysseus, Penelope and Telemachus. Thematically, it uses Odysseus's backstory and struggle as a metaphor for dealing with the aftermath of war (the novel being written immediately after the end of the Second World War).[[75]](#cite_note-Nordgren_2004-75)

In the eleventh chapter of [Primo Levi](/wiki/Primo_Levi "Primo Levi")'s 1947 memoir *[If This Is a Man](/wiki/If_This_Is_a_Man "If This Is a Man")*, "The Canto of Ulysses", the author describes the last voyage of Ulysses as told by [Dante](/wiki/Dante_Alighieri "Dante Alighieri") in *[The Inferno](/wiki/Inferno_(Dante) "Inferno (Dante)")* to a fellow-prisoner during forced labour in the Nazi concentration camp [Auschwitz](/wiki/Auschwitz "Auschwitz").

Odysseus is the hero of *The Luck of Troy* (1961) by [Roger Lancelyn Green](/wiki/Roger_Lancelyn_Green "Roger Lancelyn Green"), whose title refers to the theft of the [Palladium](/wiki/Palladium_(mythology) "Palladium (mythology)").

In [S. M. Stirling](/wiki/S._M._Stirling "S. M. Stirling")'s *[Island in the Sea of Time](/wiki/Island_in_the_Sea_of_Time "Island in the Sea of Time")* (1998), first part to his [Nantucket series](/wiki/Nantucket_series "Nantucket series") of [alternate history](/wiki/Alternate_history "Alternate history") novels, Odikweos ("Odysseus" in [Mycenaean Greek](/wiki/Mycenaean_Greek "Mycenaean Greek")) is a "historical" figure who is every bit as cunning as his legendary self and is one of the few [Bronze Age](/wiki/Bronze_Age "Bronze Age") inhabitants who discerns the time-travellers' real background. Odikweos first aids William Walker's rise to power in [Achaea](/wiki/Achaea "Achaea") and later helps bring Walker down after seeing his homeland turn into a [police state](/wiki/Police_state "Police state").

*[The Penelopiad](/wiki/The_Penelopiad "The Penelopiad")* (2005) by [Margaret Atwood](/wiki/Margaret_Atwood "Margaret Atwood") retells his story from the point of view of his wife [Penelope](/wiki/Penelope "Penelope").

[Rick Riordan](/wiki/Rick_Riordan "Rick Riordan")'s novel series *[Percy Jackson & the Olympians](/wiki/Percy_Jackson_%26_the_Olympians "Percy Jackson & the Olympians")*, which centres on the presence of Greek mythology in the 21st century, incorporates several elements from Odysseus's story. The second novel in particular, *[The Sea of Monsters](/wiki/The_Sea_of_Monsters "The Sea of Monsters")* (2006), is a loose adaptation of *The Odyssey*, with protagonists Percy and Annabeth seeking to save their satyr friend Grover from Polyphemus, and facing many of the same obstacles Odysseus faced over the course of the journey.

[Volodymyr Yermolenko](/wiki/Volodymyr_Yermolenko "Volodymyr Yermolenko"), Ukrainian philosopher and essayist, wrote *Ocean Catcher: The Story of Odysseus*, Stary Lev, 2017, which is loose adaptation of The Odyssey, where after coming back home to Ithaca, where he cannot find either Penelope or [Telemachus](/wiki/Telemachus "Telemachus"), he decides to have a reverse trip to Troy.[[76]](#cite_note-76)[[77]](#cite_note-77)

### Comparative mythology and folkloristics

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Odysseus&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Comparative mythology and folkloristics")]

Over time, comparisons between Odysseus and other heroes of different mythologies and religions have been made. A similar story exists in [Hindu mythology](/wiki/Hindu_mythology "Hindu mythology") with [Nala](/wiki/Nala "Nala") and [Damayanti](/wiki/Damayanti "Damayanti") where Nala separates from Damayanti and is reunited with her.[[85]](#cite_note-85) The story of stringing a bow is similar to the description in the *[Ramayana](/wiki/Ramayana "Ramayana")* of [Rama](/wiki/Rama "Rama") stringing the bow to win [Sita](/wiki/Sita "Sita")'s hand in marriage.[[86]](#cite_note-86)

[Virgil's *Aeneid* has evident similarities](/wiki/Parallels_between_Virgil%27s_Aeneid_and_Homer%27s_Iliad_and_Odyssey "Parallels between Virgil's Aeneid and Homer's Iliad and Odyssey") to the Odyssey. [Virgil](/wiki/Virgil "Virgil") tells the story of [Aeneas](/wiki/Aeneas "Aeneas") and his travels to what would become Rome. On his journey he endures strife comparable to that of Odysseus. However, the motives for both of their journeys differ as Aeneas was driven by this sense of duty granted to him by the gods that he must abide by. He keeps in mind the future of his people, fitting for the future *Father of Rome*.

In [folkloristics](/wiki/Folkloristics "Folkloristics"), the story of Odysseus's journey back to his native Ithaca and wife Penelope corresponds to the tale type ATU 974, ["The Homecoming Husband"](/w/index.php?title=%22The_Homecoming_Husband%22&action=edit&redlink=1 "\"The Homecoming Husband\" (page does not exist)") [[de](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heimkehr_des_Gatten "de:Heimkehr des Gatten")], of the international [Aarne–Thompson–Uther Index](/wiki/Aarne%E2%80%93Thompson%E2%80%93Uther_Index "Aarne–Thompson–Uther Index") for folktale classification.[[87]](#cite_note-87)[[88]](#cite_note-88)[[89]](#cite_note-89)[[90]](#cite_note-90)

Role as a figure of worship
---------------------------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Odysseus&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Role as a figure of worship")]

Evidence suggests the existence of a cult dedicated to Odysseus on Ithaca. This evidence includes public games called the Odysseia (τά Ὀδύσσεια) and a designated public gathering place[[91]](#cite_note-91) or a sanctuary,[[92]](#cite_note-92) known as the Odysseion (τό Ὀδύσσειον).
In 2025, researchers identified what is believed to be the sanctuary of Odysseus at the site Agios Athanasios–School of Homer in northern Ithaca (known since the 19th century as the "School of Homer". Two late Hellenistic inscriptions were discovered bearing "ΟΔΥCCEOC" (genitive) and "ΟΔΥCCEI" (dative). These align with a 1930s inscription from the Polis Bay cave reading "ΕΥΧΗΝ ΟΔΥCCΕΙ" ("Thanks Odysseus"). Additional finds, such as a miniature bronze bust of Odysseus, 34 clay votive fragments, loom weights, jewelry, and over 100 coins, highlight the site's religious and social role during the Hellenistic and early Roman periods (3rd century BCE – 2nd century CE). The lower terrace, featuring architectural remains, carved dedication niches, and roof tiles inscribed with references to [Apollo](/wiki/Apollo "Apollo") Agyieus and the symbol "ΔΗ" (which may indicate "public"), confirms the site's function in formal religious rituals. This indicates that the sanctuary catered to both local devotees and visiting pilgrims.[[93]](#cite_note-93)

[Strabo](/wiki/Strabo "Strabo") writes that on Meninx ([Ancient Greek](/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Μῆνιγξ) island, modern [Djerba](/wiki/Djerba "Djerba") at [Tunisia](/wiki/Tunisia "Tunisia"), there was an altar to Odysseus.[[94]](#cite_note-94)

[Pliny the Elder](/wiki/Pliny_the_Elder "Pliny the Elder") writes that in Italy there were some small islands (modern Torricella, Praca, Brace and other rocks)[[95]](#cite_note-95) which were called Ithacesiae because of a watchtower that Odysseus built there.[[96]](#cite_note-96)

According to ancient Greek tradition, Odysseus founded a city in [Iberia](/wiki/Iberia "Iberia") which was called Odysseia (Ὀδύσσεια)[[97]](#cite_note-Strabo,_3.2.13-97)[[98]](#cite_note-Strabo,_3.4.3-98) or Odysseis (Ὀδυσσεῖς)[[99]](#cite_note-99) which had a sanctuary of goddess [Athena](/wiki/Athena "Athena").[[97]](#cite_note-Strabo,_3.2.13-97)[[98]](#cite_note-Strabo,_3.4.3-98)[[100]](#cite_note-Dictionary_of_Greek_and_Roman_Geography-100) Ancient authors identified it with [Olisipo](/wiki/Olisipo "Olisipo") (modern [Lisbon](/wiki/Lisbon "Lisbon")), but modern researchers believe that even its existence is uncertain.[[100]](#cite_note-Dictionary_of_Greek_and_Roman_Geography-100)

[Hellanicus of Lesbos](/wiki/Hellanicus_of_Lesbos "Hellanicus of Lesbos") wrote that [Rome](/wiki/Rome "Rome") was founded by Aeneas and Odysseus who came together there. Other ancient historians, including [Damastes of Sigeum](/wiki/Damastes_of_Sigeum "Damastes of Sigeum"), agreed with him.[[101]](#cite_note-101)[[102]](#cite_note-102)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

***A Treatise of Civil Power*** was published by the English poet and [polemicist](/wiki/Polemicist "Polemicist") [John Milton](/wiki/John_Milton "John Milton") in February 1659. The work argues over the definition and nature of [heresy](/wiki/Heresy "Heresy") and [free thought](/wiki/Free_thought "Free thought"), and Milton tries to convince the new [English Parliament](/wiki/English_Parliament "English Parliament") to further his cause.

The work is addressed the work to the [Lord Protector](/wiki/Lord_Protector "Lord Protector") [Richard Cromwell](/wiki/Richard_Cromwell "Richard Cromwell"). Milton expresses his belief that an individual's conscience was more important than any external factors or forces, advocating [freedom of religion](/wiki/Freedom_of_religion "Freedom of religion") or the ability of people to voluntarily choose their own religious affiliation. In context, he opposed any form of [state religion](/wiki/State_religion "State religion").

Background
----------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")]

*A Treatise of Civil Power in Ecclesiastical Causes* was published in February 1659 after [Richard Cromwell](/wiki/Richard_Cromwell "Richard Cromwell") established a new Parliament. Milton addresses the tract to Cromwell and Parliament because he was afraid of the various positions of the [Interregnum](/wiki/Interregnum "Interregnum") government that promoted intolerance and limited the free speech of individuals (like Milton himself).[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Tract
-----

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Tract")]

Although Milton knew that the word "heresy" was used as a pejorative, Milton believed that the term was properly defined[[2]](#cite_note-2) as "only the choice or following of any opinion good or bad in religion or any other learning".[[3]](#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3) Furthermore, he argues that a man is only moved "by the inward persuasive motions of his spirit".[[4]](#cite_note-4)

The text is primarily concerned about the covenants formed between men and of agreements:[[5]](#cite_note-5) "Let who so will interpret or determine, so it be according to true church; which is exercis'd on them only who have willingly joined themselves in that covnant of union".[[3]](#cite_note-Milton_p._246-3)

Themes
------

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=A_Treatise_of_Civil_Power&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Themes")]

Milton believed that an individual's conscience was more important than any external factors or forces.[[6]](#cite_note-6) He uses heresy in a neutral manner in order to place the concept as an obligation of true Christians.[[7]](#cite_note-7) The work, according to John Shawcross, is like other of his later works in that it contains "A fusion of submission and revolution".[[8]](#cite_note-8) Thomas Corns believes the language of the text is subdued, comparatively speaking, and contains little of the powers of language found within Milton's earlier prose.[[9]](#cite_note-9) Conversely, [Kevin Hart](/wiki/Kevin_Hart_(poet) "Kevin Hart (poet)") wrote in *[First Things](/wiki/First_Things "First Things")*, "His powerful attack against the idea of a state church remains one of the most pungent pieces of prose in the language."[[10]](#cite_note-10)

He and his wife were buried in one tomb which was shown in the city of [Amphissa](/wiki/Amfissa \"Amfissa\").[[3]](#cite_note-3)\\n* Andraemon, brother of [Leonteus](/wiki/Leonteus_(mythology) \"Leonteus (mythology)\").
